evidence.title: Equity and AI governance at academic medical centers
evidence.venue: The American journal of managed care
evidence.outcome: Whether equity is considered in AI governance processes at academic medical centers
evidence.effect: A minority of participants reported considering inequity, racism, or bias in governance; a lack of consistent equity consideration was found among academic medical centers developing governance for predictive technologies.
evidence.quote: We found a lack of consistent equity consideration among academic medical centers as they develop their governance processes for predictive technologies despite considerable national attention to the ways these technologies can cause or reproduce inequities.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (chief medical informatics officers and similar) from 13 academic medical centers

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether a structured equity impact assessment before AI adoption reduces differential harm to subgroups, although several endorsing sources, including a multi-society radiology statement and a primary care commentary that describes a prospective health equity impact assessment tool, call for attention to disparities before deployment. One qualitative study of 13 academic medical centers found that only a minority of governance leaders reported considering inequity, racism, or bias.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single supplied study documents the hazard and does not evaluate an assessment. It is qualitative, with 17 interview participants from 13 academic medical centers, which limits directness and precision. The endorsements rest on expert consensus and commentary, not outcome data.

Interviews with 17 informatics leaders at 13 academic medical centers found that a minority reported weighing inequity, racism, or bias during AI governance. This suggests the gap the recommendation targets exists in practice. The study cannot show whether a pre-adoption assessment would change which tools are adopted or whether subgroup outcomes would improve.

The interview study found no consistent approach to equity review among academic centers building governance for predictive tools. That finding suggests assessments are not yet embedded in routine intake workflows. No supplied study measures the staff time, data requirements, or fidelity of a structured equity assessment when governance committees apply one to each tool.

The HEAAL framework advises organizations to track federal regulators, state attorneys general, and health departments, which may signal that oversight of AI in health care is evolving. The supplied sources do not cite a specific statute that requires pre-adoption equity assessment, and no study examines whether such assessments reduce legal or civil-rights exposure.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study compares health systems or AI tools with and without a structured pre-adoption equity impact assessment. Future work could measure whether assessments change adoption decisions, alter tool configuration, or reduce performance gaps and outcome differences across racial, language, insurance, and literacy subgroups after deployment. It could also record the staff time and data such assessments require.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study drew only on leaders at academic medical centers, did not include safety-net hospitals, and did not report on Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. How equity review functions in settings that serve these groups remains unmeasured, and those settings may have fewer resources to conduct it.
